outcome: No accepted resolution found. One single-author preprint, Nikolaev arXiv:2512.02232 (1 Dec 2025), claims to prove the full problem (infinitely many real quadratic fields with class number one); its infinitude step is the point the judging pass must check, and I found no public engagement with it. The other post-January-2024 items are finiteness results for subclasses, a family result with finitely many exceptions, or conditional results, and Wikipedia (last edited 20 July 2026 per the fetched page) still lists the problem as open.
problem_asks: Whether there are infinitely many real quadratic number fields K = Q(√d), d > 0, whose ring of integers has unique factorization. Parts: (1) the fields are real quadratic; (2) the ring of integers O_K is a UFD, which for a number field is equivalent to class number h_K = 1 and to O_K being a PID; (3) whether the set of such fields is infinite (a finite answer would also settle it). The statement names no bound on h_K, no discriminant range, and no other quantity. Wikipedia's wording says unique factorization rather than class number one; for rings of integers of number fields these coincide, so both readings are recorded.

events.what_happened: András Biró, ‘Chowla's conjecture’, Acta Arithmetica 107 (2003) 179–194, DOI 10.4064/aa107-2-5. Per search snippets of later secondary sources (article not read), it determines the square-free fields Q(√(4m²+1)) with class number one: m in {1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 13}, unconditionally. Only the publisher metadata page was opened.
events.delivers: Complete determination of class-number-one fields in the one-parameter family Q(√(4m²+1)) with square-free 4m²+1 (per secondary sources, not verified against the article). Restricted to that family.
events.remains: Every other family, and the general question of whether infinitely many real quadratic fields have class number one.
events.directly_checkable: Each field in the family could be checked by a class-number computation; not done here.
events.direction: Finite list for a restricted family; does not move the general infinitude question.

events.what_happened: András Biró, ‘Yokoi's conjecture’, Acta Arithmetica 106 (2003) 85–104. Per search snippets of later sources (article not read): class number one for Q(√(n²+4)) (square-free n²+4) occurs only for n in {1, 3, 5, 7, 13, 17}, giving the discriminants 5, 13, 29, 53, 173, 293, and h > 1 for n > 17. A 2025 arXiv paper states the result for odd n, and sources differ on the even case. A 2024 Biró talk slide snippet (unreadable to me) says the argument does not prove Yokoi's conjecture; see disputes.
events.delivers: Per secondary sources: complete list of class-number-one fields in the family Q(√(n²+4)), six square-free discriminants. Not verified against the article.
events.remains: All other families, and the general question.
events.directly_checkable: Each field in the family could be checked by class-number computation; not done.
events.doubts: Whether the published result covers even n as well as odd n is not settled by the sources I saw (Rudnick's 2026 paper relies on it through genus theory for the cases it needs).
events.direction: Finite list for a restricted family; does not move the general infinitude question.

events.what_happened: Kostadinka Lapkova, doctoral thesis ‘Class Number Problems for Quadratic Fields’, Central European University, 2012 (CEU eTD record; search snippet only, not opened). Per the snippet: treats the two-parameter family d = (an)² + 4a with a, n positive odd; shows no class-number-one fields in the subfamily where n is divisible by 43·181·353; describes this as the first unconditional result for two-parameter Richaud–Degert discriminants.
events.delivers: Per snippet: no class-number-one fields in the subfamily with n divisible by 43·181·353 of the two-parameter family d = (an)² + 4a.
events.remains: The rest of the two-parameter family, which the 2015/2016 Biró–Lapkova paper addresses, and the general question.
events.direction: Restricted subfamily; finite; does not move the general question.

events.what_happened: András Biró and Kostadinka Lapkova, ‘The class number one problem for the real quadratic fields Q(√((an)²+4a))’, arXiv:1508.05644 (v1 submitted 23 Aug 2015; one version on the arXiv page). Published in Acta Arithmetica 172 (2016) 117–131 (journal details from a search snippet, not read on the publisher page). Abstract as read on arXiv: ‘We solve unconditionally the class number one problem for the 2-parameter family of real quadratic fields Q(√d) with square-free discriminant d = (an)² + 4a for positive odd integers a and n.’
events.revisions: arXiv v1 23 Aug 2015 only; journal version Acta Arithmetica 172 (2016).
events.delivers: Complete unconditional determination of class-number-one fields in the two-parameter family d = (an)² + 4a with a, n odd and d square-free. A 2026 secondary paper (not verified) says h(d) > 1 for such d > 1253, which would make the list finite.
events.remains: Fields outside this two-parameter family, and the general infinitude question.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; referees are not named on the pages I saw

events.directly_checkable: Each field in the family could be checked by class-number computation; not done.
events.direction: Complete finite determination within a family; no bearing on whether the family set is infinite beyond the family itself.

events.what_happened: Mohit Mishra, ‘Lower bound for class number of certain real quadratic fields’, arXiv:1906.09718 (v1 24 Jun 2019; v2 12 Jul 2019, current). Abstract as read: an explicit lower bound for h(n²+r), r = 1, 4, and an equivalent criterion for attaining it in terms of a special value of the Dedekind zeta function; the bounds reduce the families in the Chowla and Yokoi conjectures to a smaller subfamily; and ‘an equivalent criteria for having an alternate proof of both the conjectures’. No journal reference found.
events.revisions: v1 24 Jun 2019; v2 12 Jul 2019 (current; same length, 13 KB).
events.delivers: Lower bound for h(n²+r) with r = 1, 4, and a reduction of the Chowla and Yokoi families to a smaller subfamily. The abstract claims a criterion for an alternate proof, not a proof. Restricted to the n²+1 and n²+4 families.
events.remains: The Chowla and Yokoi conjectures in full (not claimed as proved in the abstract), and the general question.
events.doubts: The abstract claims only an equivalent criterion for an alternate proof, but a secondary source (emergentmind open-problems snippet) says the paper yields a new proof of Chowla's and Yokoi's conjectures. I did not check whether the criterion is met. No journal publication found.
events.direction: Partial: lower bounds and family reduction; no resolution claimed in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Dongho Byeon and Jigu Kim, ‘Class number problem for a family of real quadratic fields’, Acta Arithmetica 201 (2021) 207–217, DOI 10.4064/aa210122-19-5, published online 28 Oct 2021. Abstract as read on the IMPAN page: the class number problem for a family of infinitely many real quadratic fields can be reduced to a finite computation, using an effectively computable lower bound for real quadratic class numbers from another paper by the authors (J. Number Theory, online 2020).
events.delivers: Reduction of the class-number-one question for an unnamed infinite family of real quadratic fields to a finite computation. The abstract does not say the finite computation was done or what it returned.
events.remains: The outcome of the finite computation for that family (not stated in the abstract); every other field; the general question.
events.direction: Reduction within an unidentified family; says nothing on whether infinitely many fields have class number one.

events.what_happened: András Biró, ‘Class number one problem for a family of real quadratic fields’, Mathematika 68(4) (2022) 1221–1232, DOI 10.1112/mtk.12164. Received 13 Apr 2022, revised 24 Jun 2022, accepted 9 Jul 2022 (search snippet of the Wiley page; the Wiley page returned HTTP 403 to my fetch). Abstract excerpt as read on the REAL repository page: ‘We effectively solve the class number one problem for a certain family.’ Per a search snippet of the author's accepted-manuscript PDF (unreadable to my fetch tool): the family is indexed by an infinite set of odd positive fundamental discriminants containing the Yokoi discriminants n²+4, so it generalizes the solution of Yokoi's conjecture, and may include fields whose fundamental unit is as large as log²D.
events.delivers: Effective, unconditional determination of class-number-one fields in an infinite family of real quadratic fields Q(√D), D in an infinite set of odd positive fundamental discriminants containing n²+4. Restricted to that family, which the snippet says may include fields with large fundamental units.
events.remains: Fields outside the family, and the general question of whether infinitely many real quadratic fields have class number one.

checked_by.who: Mathematika (London Mathematical Society / Wiley), refereed journal
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper after revision (accepted 9 Jul 2022 per the Wiley snippet)

events.direction: Restricted family; finite determination; does not bear on infinitude outside the family.

events.what_happened: Malik Amir, Yang-Hui He, Kyu-Hwan Lee, Thomas Oliver and Eldar Sultanow, ‘Machine Learning Class Numbers of Real Quadratic Fields’, arXiv:2209.09283 (submitted 19 Sep 2022, v1 only); International Journal of Data Science in the Mathematical Sciences 1(2) (2023) 107–134, DOI 10.1142/S2810939223500016. Abstract as read: ‘We implement and interpret various supervised learning experiments involving real quadratic fields with class numbers 1, 2 and 3’; feature analysis, PCA, and ‘symbolic classification to develop machine-learned formulas for class numbers 1, 2 and 3 that apply to our dataset.’ A search snippet also reports a 2020 He–Lee–Oliver random-forest classifier on Dedekind zeta coefficients (not opened).
events.revisions: v1 only (19 Sep 2022) on the arXiv page; journal version 2023.
events.delivers: Empirical only: classifiers and fitted formulas on a finite dataset of real quadratic fields with class numbers 1, 2 and 3. The abstract claims no theorem about infinitude and no proof.
events.remains: Everything: the abstract makes no statement about whether infinitely many fields have class number one.

checked_by.who: International Journal of Data Science in the Mathematical Sciences (World Scientific)

events.directly_checkable: The fitted formulas can be tested against class-number data; not done.
events.doubts: The formulas are said to apply to the authors' dataset, not to be general theorems; the abstract does not say any result was proved from them.
events.direction: No direction on the question; data-fitted formulas for h = 1, 2, 3 on a finite dataset.

events.what_happened: András Biró, talk ‘Parametric families of real quadratic fields’, Rényi Institute seminar, 31 May 2024 (event listing seen in search; slides PDF dated 24 May 2024 by metadata, unreadable to my fetch tool). Per a search snippet of the slides (not read in full): the argument discussed does not prove Yokoi's conjecture though it comes close; it asks whether similar families with small fundamental units can be defined, and whether the class number one problem can be solved for them. No written argument found.
events.delivers: Talk only; per the snippet, a method that comes close to Yokoi's conjecture without proving it. No new result claimed in what I could see.
events.remains: Yokoi's conjecture as the talk describes it, all other families, and the general question.
events.doubts: Known only from a snippet of the slides; the slides could not be read.
events.direction: No resolution claimed; sits in the Yokoi-family dispute recorded in disputes.

events.what_happened: Dongho Byeon (Seoul National University), guest lecture ‘Real quadratic fields whose class numbers are odd, but not one’, Paris Lodron University of Salzburg, Tuesday 25 June 2024, 12:15, invitation by Clemens Fuchs. Known from a search snippet of the invitation PDF, which my fetch tool could not read. Per the snippet: the talk claims to prove there are infinitely many real quadratic fields whose class numbers are odd but not one, and it restates that infinitude of class-number-one fields among odd-class-number fields remains unproven. No written paper found.
events.delivers: Claimed in the talk announcement only: infinitely many real quadratic fields with odd class number greater than one. This concerns a different quantity from class number one.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many real quadratic fields have class number one, which the talk leaves open.
events.doubts: Known only from a seminar announcement snippet; no write-up found, so the claim cannot be assessed here.
events.direction: Not about class number one; a neighbouring claim about odd class numbers greater than one.

events.what_happened: Riccardo Bernardini, ‘Class number of real quadratic fields of explicit discriminant’, arXiv:2412.06351 (submitted 9 Dec 2024, v1 only, 21 pages, math.NT). Abstract as read: the paper studies a family of real quadratic fields for which the square roots of the discriminants have a known continued fraction expansion; ‘In particular we prove that h(D) > 1, with possibly a finite number of exceptions.’ No journal reference on the arXiv page.
events.revisions: v1 only (9 Dec 2024) on the arXiv page read on 11 Oct 2026.
events.delivers: Within the explicit-discriminant family (McLaughlin-type continued fraction construction), class number greater than one for all members except possibly finitely many, i.e. class number one occurs only finitely often in that family.
events.remains: Everything outside the family; within the family, the finitely many possible exceptions, which would be the class-number-one fields.
events.direction: Finiteness within a family, opposite in spirit to the infinitude question; not a count over all real quadratic fields.

events.what_happened: Elias Caeiro and Henri Darmon, ‘The Heegner–Stark theorem and Stark–Heegner points’, Essential Number Theory 4(1) (2025) 67–99, DOI 10.2140/ent.2025.4.67. Received 23 May 2024, revised 18 Feb 2025, accepted 19 Feb 2025, published 28 Mar 2025. No arXiv preprint found. Abstract as read: the Heegner–Baker–Stark determination of imaginary quadratic orders of class number one relies on complex multiplication; ‘A conjectural extension of this theory to real quadratic fields based on the notion of rigid analytic elliptic cocycles is shown to yield similar lists for some explicit families of real quadratic orders with small regulators.’
events.revisions: No earlier public version found; 28 Mar 2025 is the earliest public date I could establish.
events.delivers: Conditional on an unproved conjectural extension of complex multiplication theory to real quadratic fields: similar class-number-one lists for some explicit families of real quadratic orders with small regulators. Conditional and restricted to orders in explicit families.
events.remains: The unconditional real case, the families not covered, the conjectural framework itself, and the general question.

checked_by.who: Essential Number Theory (Mathematical Sciences Publishers), refereed journal

events.doubts: The real-field result rests on a conjectural framework (rigid analytic cocycles and Darmon's real multiplication programme), so it is conditional by its own abstract.
events.direction: Conditional lists for explicit families of orders; cannot settle infinitude.

events.what_happened: Riccardo Bernardini, ‘Upper bounds on class numbers of real quadratic fields’, arXiv:2506.21301 (v1 26 Jun 2025; v2 last revised 8 Aug 2026). Abstract excerpts as read: for any ε > 0 the number of real quadratic fields of the relevant size with small class number is at least x^{1/2−ε}; the bound improves by a factor log log d a 1971 result of Yamamoto; a lower bound on the fundamental unit under algebraic conditions; ‘Our proof corrects a work of Halter-Koch.’ Main theorem as read: h(d) ≪ √d / ((log d)² log log d) for at least x^{1/2−ε} fundamental discriminants 0 < d < x.
events.revisions: v1 26 Jun 2025; v2 8 Aug 2026 (arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Upper bounds on class numbers for many fundamental discriminants at large d, and a count of such discriminants. None of its statements concerns class number one: the bound exceeds 1 for large d.
events.remains: Everything in the class-number-one question; the paper does not address whether h(d) = 1 occurs infinitely often.
events.direction: Neither direction on this question: upper bounds on class numbers for a family-like set of discriminants, not an exact class-number-one statement.

events.what_happened: Igor V. Nikolaev, ‘Lambert W-function and Gauss class number one conjecture’, arXiv:2512.02232, submitted 1 Dec 2025, one version, 9 pages, math.NT with math.OA cross-list. Abstract as read on the arXiv page: the paper studies fixed points of a function arising in a representation theory of Drinfeld modules by bounded operators on a Hilbert space; ‘We prove that such points correspond to number fields of the class number one.’ ‘As an application, one gets a solution to the Gauss conjecture for the real quadratic fields of class number one.’ Real-quadratic step as returned by my fetch tool from the HTML version (Section 3.2, case (ii)): ‘Since there are infinitely many distinct values of ε, we infer from Theorem 1.1 that #{k|hk=1}=∞’, where k is real quadratic and the ε are units of O_k^× (infinite by Dirichlet's unit theorem). Corollary 1.2, as summarised by the same tool from the LaTeX (not verbatim): 8 class-number-one fields for r = 1 with k in (C−R) ∪ Q, and infinitely many for r = 1 with k real. No journal reference.
events.revisions: v1 only (1 Dec 2025) on the arXiv abstract page read on 11 Oct 2026; no comment field beyond '9 pages'.
events.delivers: As claimed, not checked: a family of number fields K ≅ k given by Lambert W formulas (1.1), with roots α in one-to-one correspondence with the units ε of real quadratic fields k, and infinitely many distinct ε, hence infinitely many real quadratic fields of class number one, which is the whole bullet. As a calibration, the paper's own Remark 1.3 (quoted in a search snippet) says its method covers the imaginary case except d = −1, i.e. 8 of the 9 known imaginary quadratic class-number-one fields, which matches the Corollary as summarised. Restrictions: none stated beyond the claim itself.
events.remains: If the argument holds, nothing of the bullet remains. If the infinitude step fails, the whole bullet remains open; the imaginary-case results do not bear on the real case.
events.directly_checkable: Each field the construction yields could be checked for class number one by standard class-number computation; I did not check any. The infinitude claim itself cannot be checked by computation.
events.doubts: (1) The infinitude step runs from infinitely many distinct units ε of one real quadratic field to infinitely many fields k with h_k = 1. The text I could read (the HTML rendering, through a fetch summary) does not show why distinct units give distinct fields. Remark 3.6 asserts k′ ≇ k ‘due to a transcendental nature of the Lambert W-function’ without proof. (2) Section 3.1 opens ‘For the sake of clarity, let us outline the main ideas’, and the same tool reports the proof of Theorem 1.1 ‘consists of a straightforward calculation’, with explicit matrix formulas deferred to a cited remark [6, Remark 6.6.3]. (3) The reference list, as read through the tool, does not cite Heilbronn, Baker, Stark, Biró, Lapkova, Watkins or Weinberger, the standard literature on this exact question, and the paper does not describe its claim as conditional. (4) The author's arXiv record in the sources I saw is in operator algebras and noncommutative geometry (arXiv:2306.06416, 2309.05779, 2509.01818); I did not review his number-theory publications. (5) Seven targeted searches found no review, journal acceptance, error report, or response. (6) The same author's arXiv:2603.24313 (25 Mar 2026, imaginary case, same Drinfeld-module method) does not mention 2512.02232 on its abstract page; its PDF was unreadable, so whether it cites this claim is unknown.
events.direction: Claims the answer the bullet's question points to: infinitely many real quadratic fields with class number one (the ‘yes’ answer that Cohen–Lenstra heuristics also predict).
events.object: No single exhibited field. The construction takes formulas (1.1) defining number fields K ≅ k from roots α of an equation of the form z = A + B·e^{Cz}, solved by the Lambert W function (Lemma 2.1), with the roots indexed by units ε of real quadratic k. Infinitude is by counting roots, not by a list of discriminants. The construction is explicit in its formulas, but the paper's real-field infinitude is non-constructive in the sense that no infinite list of fields is written down.

events.what_happened: Gene S. Kopp and Jeffrey C. Lagarias, ‘Unit-generated orders of real quadratic fields I. Class number bounds’, arXiv:2512.11311 (v1 12 Dec 2025; v2 21 Dec 2025; v3 21 Apr 2026, comment ‘v3 adds proof of complete list of unit-generated quadratic orders of class number 1’). Abstract as read: unit-generated orders are parametrized as O_n^± with discriminants n² − 4 (n ≥ 3) and n² + 4 (n ≥ 1); their class numbers satisfy log|Cl(O)| ~ log(½|Δ|) as |Δ| → ∞, via a result of L.-K. Hua; ‘We deduce that there are finitely many unit-generated quadratic orders of class number one’; they ‘classify all unit-generated real quadratic orders having class number one’; numerical lists to Δ ≤ 10^10 are ‘conjecturally complete for all Δ’.
events.revisions: v1 12 Dec 2025; v2 21 Dec 2025; v3 21 Apr 2026 (current, 31 KB).
events.delivers: Finiteness: only finitely many unit-generated real quadratic orders have class number one, and they are classified (per v3). Restricted to orders generated by units; says nothing about orders or fields outside that class.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many real quadratic fields have class number one, with no unit-generated restriction.
events.directly_checkable: Numerical lists for Δ ≤ 10^10 are checkable by class-group computation; not done.
events.doubts: The numerical lists are conjecturally complete beyond Δ ≤ 10^10 (the authors' conjecture, not a theorem). No error found.
events.direction: Finiteness for a subclass; cuts against infinitude only within unit-generated orders and does not move the field question.

events.what_happened: Kalyan Banerjee, Ankurjyoti Chutia and Azizul Hoque, ‘On the simultaneous 3-divisibility of class numbers of quadruples of real quadratic fields’, arXiv:2512.11346 (v1 12 Dec 2025). Abstract as read: ‘we construct infinitely many quadruples of real quadratic fields whose class numbers are all divisible by 3’, with an application to elliptic curves with a 3-torsion subgroup.
events.delivers: Infinitely many quadruples of real quadratic fields with all class numbers divisible by 3. This concerns divisibility, not class number one.
events.remains: The entire class-number-one question.
events.direction: Neither direction on this question; a divisibility result on a different quantity.

events.what_happened: Farahnaz Amiri, ‘Computing p-Class Group Structure in Real Quadratic Fields: A New Approach’, arXiv:2601.19288 (v1 27 Jan 2026, one version). Abstract as read: ‘This article is the first in a series devoted to computing the class groups of real quadratic fields.’ It presents a new relation between the class number and the index of unit groups, generalizing Hilbert class field theory for real quadratic fields, and links to composition laws of binary forms of degree p^n.
events.delivers: A relation between class numbers and unit indices, for p-class groups; no class-number-one statement in the abstract.
events.remains: The entire class-number-one question.
events.direction: Neither direction on this question; a methods paper on class groups.

events.what_happened: Evan Chen, Chris Cummins, Ben Eltschig, Dejan Grubisic, Leopold Haller, Letong Hong, Andranik Kurghinyan, Kenny Lau, Hugh Leather, Seewoo Lee, Aram Markosyan, Ken Ono, Manooshree Patel, Gaurang Pendharkar, Vedant Rathi, Alex Schneidman, Volker Seeker, Shubho Sengupta, Ishan Sinha, Jimmy Xin and Jujian Zhang, ‘Almost all primes are partially regular’, arXiv:2602.05090 (submitted 4 Feb 2026, one version). A neighbouring problem, not this one: it concerns the eigenspaces of the p-Sylow subgroup of Cl(Q(ζ_p)) and proves that a density-one set of primes is partially regular, yielding a partial Vandiver theorem. The abstract, as fetched, says the theorem ‘is fully formalized in Lean/Mathlib and was produced automatically by AxiomProver from a natural-language statement of the conjecture’. The Lean package (Lean Reservoir, not opened) reports Lean 4.26.0. Axiom's blog post (search snippet, not opened) says AxiomProver also translated the statement into Lean.
events.delivers: For cyclotomic fields Q(ζ_p): a density-one set of primes is partially regular, giving a partial Vandiver theorem. Nothing about real quadratic class numbers.
events.remains: The whole class-number-one question for real quadratic fields.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 with Mathlib (Lean 4.26.0 per the Lean Reservoir package snippet)

events.doubts: Peer review status unknown; the Lean build's sorry status was not checked. The AI sentence is quoted from the abstract as returned by my fetch tool and should be checked verbatim against arXiv:2602.05090.
events.direction: No direction on this question; it addresses a neighbouring class-group question for cyclotomic fields.

systems.what_it_did: Per the abstract as fetched: produced the proof of partial regularity for almost all primes automatically from a natural-language statement, and the theorem is fully formalized in Lean/Mathlib. Applies to the neighbouring cyclotomic problem, not to real quadratic class numbers.

events.what_happened: Sören Sprehe, ‘Antisymmetry of real quadratic singular moduli’, arXiv:2603.09764 (v1 10 Mar 2026; v2 8 Oct 2026). Abstract as read: confirms a conjecture of Darmon–Vonk on the antisymmetry of real quadratic singular moduli, using rigid meromorphic cocycles for the orthogonal group of a quaternion algebra, and proves modularity of a generating series of Kudla–Millson divisors.
events.delivers: Antisymmetry of real quadratic singular moduli. Not a statement about class numbers.
events.remains: The entire class-number-one question. It touches the Darmon–Vonk real-multiplication programme on which the conditional results (Caeiro–Darmon, Caeiro 2026) rest, but the abstract does not connect it to those.
events.direction: Neither direction on this question; a neighbouring result on singular moduli.

events.what_happened: Elias Caeiro (Princeton), with Henri Darmon and Jingxuan Geng, talk ‘Heegner points, Stark-Heegner points and class number problems’, Ohio State Harmonic Analysis and Automorphic Representations seminar, Monday 23 March 2026, 4–5 pm (event page opened). Abstract as read: the method determines all negative discriminants of class number at most 3 geometrically, without Goldfeld's analytic method; ‘Assuming Darmon's conjectural real multiplication theory, this method can be adapted to determine all real quadratic fields of Richaud–Degert type which have class number one, giving a conditional improvement on work of Biró and Lapkova.’ No written paper found.
events.delivers: Conditional on Darmon's conjectural real multiplication theory: a determination of all real quadratic fields of Richaud–Degert type with class number one. Restricted to Richaud–Degert type and conditional. The imaginary part (class number at most 3) is unconditional but outside this bullet's real case.
events.remains: The unconditional real case, fields outside Richaud–Degert type, and the general infinitude question.
events.doubts: Conditional on a conjectural theory the abstract names; known only from the seminar abstract, with no written argument found.
events.direction: Conditional finite classification for a restricted family; does not address infinitude.

events.what_happened: Zeev Rudnick, ‘The classification of real quadratic fields which satisfy Hammarhjelm's condition’, arXiv:2606.31544 (submitted 30 Jun 2026, v1 only, math.NT with math.DS cross-list). Abstract as read: a real quadratic field satisfies Hammarhjelm's condition if its ring of integers has unique factorization and the Minkowski lattice contains no point in a certain rectangle determined by the fundamental unit; ‘We prove that there are exactly seven real quadratic fields satisfying Hammarhjelm's condition, namely those with discriminant 8, 5, 13, 29, 53, 173, 293.’ The proof uses that the fundamental unit is small relative to the discriminant, genus theory, and Biró's classification of class number one fields in Yokoi's family.
events.delivers: Exactly seven real quadratic fields that have unique factorization and satisfy an extra lattice condition. A finiteness result for a restricted subclass of the UFD fields; the extra condition arises in visible-point counting in cut-and-project sets.
events.remains: All real quadratic fields with unique factorization that fail the extra condition, and the infinitude question.
events.directly_checkable: The seven fields are checkable by class-number and fundamental-unit computation; not done.
events.direction: Finiteness within a restricted subclass; neither proves nor disproves the general statement.
events.object: The seven fields, listed by discriminant 8, 5, 13, 29, 53, 173, 293, with the classification proof through the fundamental unit bound and genus theory.

disputes.summary: Nikolaev arXiv:2512.02232 claims a solution of the real-quadratic Gauss conjecture (1 Dec 2025). Wikipedia (last edited 20 July 2026 per the fetched page), the emergentmind open-problems page (which quotes ‘which is still open’), and Caeiro's March 2026 talk all treat the real case as open. No refutation or acceptance was found, so the status is contested only in the sense that one claim exists.

Yokoi's conjecture. Secondary sources (search snippets, not read) say Biró proved it in 2003 and his 2022 paper ‘generalizes the solution of Yokoi's conjecture’. A 2024 Biró talk slide snippet (unreadable to me) says the argument ‘does not prove Yokoi's conjecture, though it comes close’. The two accounts are not reconciled; the 2003 paper and the 2024 slides were not read.

Mishra arXiv:1906.09718: the abstract offers ‘equivalent criteria for having an alternate proof of both the conjectures’, while a secondary source (emergentmind snippet) says it yields a new proof of Chowla's and Yokoi's conjectures. The abstract makes no proof claim.

Yokoi family counts: six fields (square-free d in {5, 13, 29, 53, 173, 293}) against ten discriminants n²+4 with class number one (5, 8, 13, 20, 29, 53, 68, 125, 173, 293) in Caeiro–Darmon's survey. The gap appears to be a convention (square-free d versus fundamental discriminants), which I did not check.

Which Gauss statement the bullet means. Gauss's 1801 Article 304 surmise concerns one-class-per-genus discriminants and, per a search snippet, allows non-fundamental discriminants, so the original version was settled long ago. The modern real-field version (fundamental discriminants, class number one, infinitely many fields) is the one Wikipedia lists as open. Wikipedia's list also carries a separate ‘solved’ Gauss item (Heilbronn 1934) about imaginary fields.

summary: Forty-five web searches (plus targeted opening of the pages they surfaced) found no accepted resolution of the problem and no AI involvement in it. The one claimed resolution is Nikolaev, arXiv:2512.02232 (1 Dec 2025), a single-version, single-author preprint whose abstract says ‘one gets a solution to the Gauss conjecture for the real quadratic fields of class number one’. Its infinitude step, as returned by my fetch tool from Section 3.2, is ‘Since there are infinitely many distinct values of ε, we infer from Theorem 1.1 that #{k|hk=1}=∞’. I could not confirm from the readable text why infinitely many units of real quadratic fields give infinitely many fields with class number one. The PDF was unreadable to my tool, so the real-field argument rests on an HTML rendering read through a summariser, and the quotes need checking verbatim. I found no commentary, review, error report or citing paper engaging with it across seven targeted searches. The same author's March 2026 paper (arXiv:2603.24313, imaginary case) was checked only on its abstract page. Wikipedia (last edited 20 July 2026 per the fetched page) still lists the problem as open. The other post-2024 items do not move the question. Bernardini's December 2024 result is a finiteness statement within one family, with finitely many possible exceptions; his June 2025 paper gives upper bounds on class numbers and says nothing about h = 1. Banerjee et al. (Dec 2025) concern 3-divisibility; Amiri (Jan 2026) concerns class-group computation. Kopp and Lagarias (Dec 2025, v3 Apr 2026) prove finitely many unit-generated orders have class number one, a restricted class. Rudnick (Jun 2026) finds exactly seven real quadratic fields satisfying Hammarhjelm's condition, a unique-factorization field with an extra lattice condition. Caeiro and Darmon (published Mar 2025) and Caeiro's talk (Mar 2026) give lists or determinations conditional on a conjectural real-multiplication theory. Pre-window family results (Biró 2003 Chowla and Yokoi families; Lapkova 2012; Biró and Lapkova 2015/2016; Mishra 2019; Byeon and Kim 2021; Biró 2022 in Mathematika) each settle a finite list or a reduction within a family. The 2022 Mathematika paper is an unconditional effective determination for an infinite family containing Yokoi's n²+4 case, and the rest of the problem remains open on all sources I read. Close calls: (a) whether the Nikolaev claim should be treated as an unverified resolution or as no resolution yet; the record carries both readings and the judging pass should decide on the infinitude step. (b) Whether the family results count as partial progress; none bears on infinitude outside its family. (c) The Yokoi dispute between secondary sources saying Biró proved it in 2003 and a 2024 talk snippet saying the argument ‘does not prove’ it; I could not read either primary source. (d) Mishra's abstract offers criteria only, while a secondary source says it proves the Chowla and Yokoi conjectures. AI: no source about this problem names an AI system. Lab announcements, Tao's Erdős wiki, the Neuron list, Epoch's FrontierMath open problems (whose class-group entry concerns imaginary quadratic fields), the AIM number theory workshop list, and AlphaEvolve and LLM searches turned up nothing on real quadratic class numbers. The nearest AI item is AxiomProver's proof (arXiv:2602.05090, 4 Feb 2026) that almost all primes are partially regular, which concerns cyclotomic class groups. The 2022 machine-learning study by Amir et al. fitted formulas for class numbers 1, 2 and 3 on a dataset, claiming no proof. For most of the events above I read the abstract or summary only, and I flag each such case in the individual entry and in incomplete.
competing_reading: The strongest case that the Nikolaev preprint is a real resolution: it makes an explicit, checkable-in-principle claim; its method reproduces the known imaginary class-number-one fields except d = −1, which the authors flag themselves, suggesting the framework is calibrated; the authors assert non-isomorphism of the constructed fields (Remark 3.6); and no one has identified an error. Against it: the infinitude step, as quoted, moves from infinitely many units of a single real quadratic field to infinitely many fields with class number one, and I could not find the justification for that move in the text I could read. The paper also does not cite the standard literature on the real case and is ten months old with no engagement found. A second reading treats the other post-2024 items as irrelevant to infinitude, which I think is right, but the Kopp–Lagarias finiteness and Rudnick classification show the field of restricted results is active, so a judging pass that counts restricted finiteness as progress would need to decide that explicitly.
what_would_settle_it: A referee report or journal decision on arXiv:2512.02232, or a version 2 that repairs or withdraws the units-to-fields step; a specialist's written analysis of Section 3.2 showing whether the roots and units give pairwise non-isomorphic real quadratic fields with class number one, checked against explicit class-number data for the fields the construction yields; an independent paper proving or refuting infinitude of real quadratic fields with class number one; or the Nikolaev PDF text, read verbatim, to confirm the quoted sentences and Corollary 1.2.

events.credibility_reason: Sources disagree on whether the even-n case is covered, and a 2024 talk snippet says the argument does not prove Yokoi's conjecture.

Several F10 signals together: a landmark claim with no engagement found after ~10 months; Wikipedia (July 2026) and Caeiro's March 2026 talk still treat the real case as open; the author's record is in operator algebras, not this literature, which the paper does not cite; the key infinitude step goes from infinitely many units to infinitely many class-number-one fields with no visible justification (non-isomorphism only asserted in Remark 3.6); the proof is described as an outline and a 'straightforward calculation' in a 9-page paper.
events.direction: confirmed

events.ai_basis: was produced automatically by AxiomProver from a natural-language statement of the conjecture

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether infinitely many real quadratic fields have class number one. Family results (Biró, Lapkova, Biró–Lapkova, Bernardini 2024, Kopp–Lagarias, Rudnick) prove finiteness inside a restricted family. That answers a different question: 'finitely many in family F' leaves the infinitude question untouched either way. So I scored them variant rather than case. Conditional results (Caeiro–Darmon, Caeiro talk), neighbouring quantities (odd class numbers, 3-divisibility, upper bounds, cyclotomic regularity, singular moduli) are variant as well. Reductions, methods papers and the ML study are none. Nikolaev is the only claim on the whole question. Taken together, several signals make it not_credible: no uptake, later sources still call the problem open, the author works outside the field and does not cite its literature, and the key units-to-fields step has an unexplained gap. No specific public refutation exists, so it is not knocked_down. AxiomProver's event is genuinely AI-generated by its own quote, but it is about cyclotomic fields, so it is variant and carries no credit for this problem. Amir et al. used ML for data fitting with no systems listed, so it is none.
judgement.doubts: Scoring family-finiteness results as variant rather than case is the main close call; either way none of them bears on the infinitude question. The Nikolaev quotes come from a summarising fetch of the HTML, not a verbatim read. not_credible versus doubtful turns on the unexplained infinitude step, which the record identifies but no expert has publicly confirmed as an error.
